Barnaby Badger grumbled. "Oh, my aching back!" He stood at the entrance to his burrow, trying to stretch. "If I don't get this bed sorted, I shall be a miserable badger indeed when the first snow falls."

Just then, Poppy Rabbit came hopping down the path, her ears twitching with cheer.

"A fine day, Mr. Badger!" she called out.

"Fine for some, perhaps," Barnaby huffed. "It is not fine for my back. I need to gather bedding, but I can hardly bend." He looked at the spry young rabbit. "You wouldn't be so kind as to help an old badger, would you? I need the very _softest_ bedding you can find."

"Of course!" Poppy exclaimed, delighted to be of service. "The softest bedding there is! I know just the thing!" And she hopped away in a flash, her white tail bobbing.

Barnaby Badger waited, and he was quite surprised to see her return so quickly, followed by all her little brothers and sisters. Each one was dragging a great bundle of sweet-smelling clover, still damp with morning dew. They piled it in a heap before the badger's door.

"There!" Poppy said proudly. "Is it not the best? There is no softer food, and every one knows the best food makes the best bed!"

Barnaby Badger stared. "Clover!" he roared, and the little rabbits jumped. "_Wet clover_? Do you think I am a cow? I asked for _bedding_, not a salad!"

"But it's the softest!" Poppy insisted, her ears drooping.

"It's the wettest!" Barnaby retorted. "I'd catch a terrible chill! I wanted dry moss and soft leaves, not this soggy mess. You must have fluff for brains!"

Poor Poppy's nose trembled, and she quickly gathered her siblings and scurried away, leaving the badger to stare crossly at the pile of clover.

Of course, Mrs. Magpie had been watching the whole affair from a branch overhead. "Did you hear?" she chattered to everyone she met in the Elderberry Patch. "Barnaby Badger is filling his home with rotting weeds! He told Poppy Rabbit he wants to sleep in a damp, smelly swamp all winter!"

By the time the story reached old Papa Mole, it was said that Barnaby Badger was digging a swimming pool in his burrow and had ordered all the rabbits to fill it with mud.

Later that afternoon, a very shamefaced Poppy Rabbit appeared again at Barnaby's door. Behind her was a long line of rabbits, each carrying a bundle of the driest, fluffiest moss and crispest, cleanest oak leaves.

"I am very sorry, Mr. Badger," Poppy said quietly. "I told my mother what you said. And she explained that what is soft to a rabbit is not always soft to a badger."

Barnaby Badger looked from Poppy's face to the beautiful pile of proper bedding. His grumpy expression softened just a little. "Well," he said, clearing his throat. "I suppose I was a bit hasty. I did not mean you had fluff for brains."

"Then," Poppy asked, "you don't think I'm a silly rabbit?"

"No," said Barnaby. "You are a very helpful rabbit. And this," he added, patting the pile of moss, "is the very _best_ bedding in the whole wood. Now, if you would just help me carry it inside." And for the first time all day, Barnaby Badger almost smiled.

THE SEEING STONE

XIII THE GREAT GREEN SERPENT

The days grew shorter and a crispness crept into the air of Pleasant Valley. Sandy Chipmunk was busier than ever, for now the oaks were dropping their acorns and the hickory trees were heavy with nuts. His little storeroom in the stone wall was nearly full, and he spent many a fine afternoon simply rearranging his treasures, counting them, and patting the smooth, hard shells.

He had not seen much of Mr. Crow since the night on Farmer Green's barn. Sandy heard from Frisky Squirrel that Mr. Crow had been very quiet, and mostly kept to the tall pines at the edge of the woods, grumbling to himself about disrespectful weather-vanes and ignorant chipmunks. Sandy did not mind at all. A quiet Mr. Crow meant a peaceful valley.

One sunny afternoon, while Sandy was sunning himself on the flat top of the stone wall, he saw Farmer Green's wagon come rattling up the road. The farmer was returning from the village, and in the back of his wagon was something long and green and coiled, like a giant garden snake taking a nap. Farmer Green stopped his horse near the water-pump by the side of the barn, and with a good deal of grunting and pulling, he lifted the strange, sleeping creature from the wagon and set it on the ground. It lay there in a perfect green coil, with one end near the pump and the other end lying limp in the grass, finishing in a curious piece of shiny brass.

Sandy Chipmunk watched with wide eyes. He had never seen such a thing. It did not move. It did not breathe. But it looked altogether too much like a snake for his comfort. He scurried down from the wall and hid in the entrance to his home, peeking out from behind his white thunder-ball.

He did not have to wait long before he heard a frantic flapping of wings. Mr. Crow landed with a _thump_ on a high branch of the oak tree. His feathers were ruffled and his eyes were wide with what looked like honest-to-goodness fear.

"Danger!" he croaked, his voice raspy. "There is a great danger in the farmyard!"

Frisky Squirrel, who had been chasing a falling leaf nearby, scampered up the trunk of the oak. "What is it, Mr. Crow? Is Farmer Green setting traps again?"

"Worse!" Mr. Crow declared, puffing out his chest to hide his trembling. "Far worse! Farmer Green has gone and captured a monster. I saw it with my own two eyes!"

"A monster?" Frisky's own eyes grew wide with excitement.

"A _terrible_ monster," Mr. Crow said, warming to his story now that he had an audience. "It is The Great Green River-Serpent of Swift River! I have heard tales of it, but never did I think to see it here. It is a hundred feet long, and its scales are the color of poison. Farmer Green must have caught it while it slept on the riverbank and brought it here to guard his farm."

By now, several other creatures had gathered. Jasper Jay flitted to a lower branch, and a field mouse peeked from behind a tuft of grass.

"A river-serpent!" Jasper Jay chattered. "Does it breathe fire?"

"Worse!" Mr. Crow said again, for it was a good, frightening word. "It breathes water! A whole river's worth! It can knock a bird from the sky with a single spout. And its bite... well, its bite is not to be thought of." He shuddered for effect. "He has it sleeping by the pump, waiting for his command. We must all be on our guard. Do not go near the farmyard! Do not go near the barn! That is my solemn advice."

And with that dire warning, Mr. Crow flew away, calling out "Danger! Danger!" to every corner of the woods.

Of course, the story did not stop there. Jasper Jay told Fatty Coon that the serpent had two heads. Fatty Coon told his cousin that the serpent had two heads and was covered in thorns. By the time the story got back to Frisky Squirrel, after passing through half the folk in Pleasant Valley, the serpent not only had two heads and thorns, but it could also swallow a cow whole and spit out its bones.

"Did you hear?" Frisky said, finding Sandy Chipmunk polishing an acorn. "The serpent has grown! It can swallow a cow!"

"It was coiled up and sleeping when I saw it," Sandy said doubtfully. "It didn't look big enough to swallow a cow."

"Maybe it grows when it is angry," Frisky suggested, his tail twitching with a mix of fear and curiosity. "Oh, Sandy, we must go and look at it! From a safe distance, of course. From the top of the stone wall."

"I don't know, Frisky," Sandy said, tucking his acorn carefully into a corner. "Mr. Crow said not to go near the farmyard."

"Mr. Crow also said your golf ball was a thunder-ball," Frisky reminded him. "And he said the weather-vane was a golden king. He is not always right, you know."

That was true. Sandy Chipmunk thought about it for a moment. He was very, very curious about the green creature. "All right," he said at last. "But we will be very careful. And if it so much as wiggles an ear, we will run."

So the two friends crept along the top of the stone wall until they had a clear view of Farmer Green's yard. There it was. The Great Green River-Serpent, lying exactly where the farmer had left it. It was still coiled tightly, gleaming in the afternoon sun. The brass piece on its tail--or was it its head?--shone brightly.

He crept closer, and closer still, placing each paw down as if on eggshells. The air was quiet except for the buzzing of a fly and the thumping of his own heart. He reached the serpent. It smelled strange, like rubber and dust. It did not feel like scales at all; it was smooth and slightly soft. He held his twig out, his paw shaking. He raised the twig.

"_Chit-chit-chit_!" chattered Frisky Squirrel from the wall, in a panic.

He launched himself from the branch and flapped away towards the deep woods as fast as his wings could carry him, cawing in panic.

"The Serpent-Poker," Frisky gasped between giggles. "Did you see Mr. Crow fly away? His eyes were as big as acorns!"
